title: Is there such a thing as too much information?

paragraphs.text: Let us consider the letter; although postal systems date to antiquity, it was the establishment of the London Penny Post in 1680 that provided the general public with a simple and cheap service that enabled them to exchange handwritten notes from afar. To the age-old oral form of conversation was added a new, literary form. Letters had to be picked up, sorted, transported, and delivered, and the leisurely pace at which brief moved through the post moderated people's expectations of quick replies. While many letters for mundane purposes were dashed off quickly, others were composed with care, their sentences polished, their paragraphs rounded. An appreciated subtlety took precedence over speed in the composition of messages. In the 18th century, the rise of the epistolary novel (a novel told through the medium of letters) testified to the improvement in letter-writing depth and excellence that followed the introduction of the Penny Post.

The personal letter became less essential when the construction of the telephone network allowed people to communicate with their voices across distances. But it is the rise of electronic communications — email, text messaging and social networking — that has pushed the letter to the margins of correspondence and culture. Few people write letters anymore, a fact reflected in the sharp and steady decline in the volume of personal correspondence handled by the mail. The letter and its reflective way of composing, we can now see, was a passing phenomenon, fated to just a few centuries of popularity.

Our new digital messaging systems encourage quick reactions, banter, remarks and retorts: so, once again, we are shaping our style of communication to fit the medium. Designers of computer networks have pursued one overriding goal: to push as much data as quickly as possible through the system. As network bandwidth has exploded, messages and other information have flooded the online networks we depend on for most communications. Hardly a minute goes by today without the arrival of some new message or alert. Staying on top of the flow — a talent central to maintaining one's social visibility and relevance — demands a quick eye, a nimble thumb, and non-stop shifts of attention. Little time remains to compose or ponder long messages.

However, this does not mean that brief electronic dispatches can't be witty or artful as they frequently are, but in general electronic messages tend to resemble casual oral conversations more than literary composition. Whereas the speed of a literary conversation was measured in weeks or days, the speed of an electronic one is measurable in minutes or seconds. The guiding ideal of machine communication — negligible delay — has become the guiding ideal of human communication as well. Studies of online behaviour show that as networks get speedier, people become less patient with any delay in the supply or exchange of information.

Underlying and amplifying these trends in communication is the insubstantiality of electronic writing. A physical letter moved at human speed, whether it was in a mail carrier's pouch or in the trailer of a truck, and it had the weight and dimensionality of an actual object. For writer and reader alike, a letter had a tactile presence that exerted a grip on the conscious mind, but electronic messages are vaporous; they have no material form. As a result, they have only a fleeting hold on the mind.

The adoption of the computer as the favoured medium for communication is changing personal correspondence and social expectations. It is also transforming the way we think about the work of the mind. The intellectual ideal of the contemplative thinker that held cultural sway for hundreds of years has been displaced by the ideal of the high-speed processor of data. Surrounded, as we are, by a flood of messages, we want and need to think like networked computers. To this end, the next technological step, some say, is to link the computer to the mind by building a cortical interface into the human brain, or possibly by wearing a skullcap that can translate neural, or brain, signals into digital signals. Such ventures may never become reality, but they nevertheless highlight the increasingly tight symbiosis between human and machine communications. The popularity of messaging shortcuts such as 'like' buttons and emoji shows how readily we adopt the language of machines.

In the digital ointment lies a fly. Bandwidth is elastic and data can flow ever more freely through computer networks, but the brain is not so malleable. The capacity of brains is largely fixed; they are limited to about four pieces of information at any time because the business of brains is not data processing but making sense of the information they receive, and this requires attention. The time we can push more information through our brains is by reducing the time we spend attending to the information. In the public sphere we are seeing troubling signs of a deterioration in thoughtfulness and reflection, together with an easy acceptance of half-truths. This may be evidence of the toll that information overload is taking on our ability to think and speak calmly and carefully. What we need now, perhaps, is the digital equivalent of a postage stamp to slow down our communications.
